pharm: Serotonin 5-HT4 agonist; enhances acetylcholine release in myenteric plexus to increase GI motility
quick: 5-10 mg three to four times daily (historic)
15 minutes before meals and at bedtime
summary: Cisapride is a 5-HT4 prokinetic agent formerly used for gastroesophageal reflux and gastroparesis. It was withdrawn from general use in the United States in 2000 and restricted in many countries because it prolongs the QT interval and causes serious, sometimes fatal, ventricular arrhythmias (including torsades de pointes), particularly with interacting drugs or electrolyte abnormalities. Where still available it is limited to restricted-access programs with ECG and electrolyte monitoring.
indications: Symptomatic nocturnal heartburn due to gastroesophageal reflux disease (historic labeled use)
Gastroparesis and other GI dysmotility disorders (historic/off-label, restricted)

dosage.d: 10 mg four times daily, or up to 20 mg twice daily
dosage.n: Start 5 mg if needed; use lowest effective dose

dosage.d: 5-10 mg three to four times daily
dosage.n: Only with ECG and electrolyte monitoring per protocol

admin: Take 15 minutes before meals and at bedtime
Obtain baseline ECG and correct electrolytes before use
Screen for QT-prolonging drugs and CYP3A4 inhibitors before prescribing
Do not use if QTc prolonged or in cardiac disease
Available only through restricted programs in many countries
moa: Selective serotonin 5-HT4 receptor agonist that enhances acetylcholine release from the myenteric plexus, increasing lower esophageal sphincter tone and gastric/small-bowel motility; blocks hERG potassium channels, prolonging cardiac repolarization (QT).

absolute: Known QT prolongation, congenital long QT, or history of serious ventricular arrhythmia
Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs or potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., azole antifungals, macrolides, protease inhibitors)
Significant cardiac disease, including ischemia or heart failure
relative: GI hemorrhage, mechanical obstruction or perforation

preg: Safety not established; avoid in pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
lact: Excreted in human milk in small amounts; avoid during breastfeeding.
renal: Reduce dose (about half) in renal impairment to limit accumulation and arrhythmia risk.
hepatic: Reduce dose in hepatic impairment; impaired metabolism raises plasma levels and QT risk.

major: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (azole antifungals, clarithromycin/erythromycin, protease inhibitors, nefazodone) — raise cisapride levels, torsades risk
Other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, certain antidepressants) — additive arrhythmia risk
Diuretics/drugs causing hypokalemia — increase arrhythmia risk
moderate: Grapefruit juice — inhibits CYP3A4, raises levels
interactions.food: Take 15 minutes before meals; avoid grapefruit juice.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; cisapride may accelerate alcohol absorption and worsen CNS effects.
interactions.diagnostics: May accelerate gastric emptying, altering absorption of other oral drugs.

serious: Torsades de pointes and other ventricular arrhythmias (sometimes fatal)

monitoring: Review of all concomitant medications for interactions
Symptoms of palpitations, dizziness or syncope
counsel: Take 15 minutes before meals and at bedtime as directed
Tell every prescriber you take this drug because of serious interactions
Avoid grapefruit juice and report all new medicines
Seek urgent care for palpitations, fainting or dizziness
Do not exceed the prescribed dose
pearls: Withdrawn from the routine U.S. market in 2000 and restricted worldwide due to fatal QT prolongation/torsades de pointes
Where still available it is limited to restricted-access programs with mandatory ECG and electrolyte monitoring
Metabolized by CYP3A4 — co-administration with azoles, macrolides or protease inhibitors is contraindicated
Correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia before any use
Largely replaced by safer prokinetics; prescribe only when no alternative exists
missed: Take as soon as remembered before the next meal; skip if close to the next dose. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Expect GI cramping, borborygmi and urinary frequency; serious risk is QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia. Provide continuous ECG monitoring, correct electrolytes, and give supportive/antiarrhythmic care; activated charcoal if recent ingestion.
